*speaking as the farmer*

Ai, I've been working this 12 mu for more than 40 years. Same land since I was a young man. I know every corner of it — which part holds water, which part dries out fast, where the soil is better.

My land is split into two pieces. The bigger piece, about 8 mu, I do wheat in winter and maize in summer — same as most people in the village. The other 4 mu is where I put cotton. That ground has always been better for cotton, and anyway I've grown cotton there as long as I can remember. My father did too.

I can't read much, so I don't pay attention to what the extension people write on papers. I just watch my fields and talk with the neighbors. Old Wang next to me, he's been farming as long as I have, and we do things pretty much the same way. If it worked last year, I do it again this year. No reason to change what works.

**On the wheat** — I plant around the first week of October, after the White Dew weather passes. I buy seed from the agricultural store in town, the variety everyone uses. Before planting I put down one bag of compound fertilizer per mu — that's the 15-15-15 kind, 40 kg bags. Then when the wheat comes up and starts jointing in the spring, if it looks a bit yellow I top-dress with urea, maybe half a bag per mu. I water the wheat 3 times usually — once before winter so it goes into the cold with wet ground, once at jointing in March, once at flowering. If there's good rain I skip one. Pumping water from the well costs money, the meter runs and I have to pay.

**On the maize** — the minute the wheat is off the field in June, I have to get the maize in. No time to plow. I just have someone come through with the no-till planter, drops the seed and some starter fertilizer together. Then I top-dress urea at the big-trumpet stage when the maize is knee-high. Maize needs less water than wheat — I water once or twice if it's a dry summer, otherwise the rains do the work. Harvest is end of September, then I turn around and get ready for wheat again.

**On the cotton** — this is the work that keeps the family busy. I plant after Qingming Festival when the soil is warm, mid to late April. Cotton takes less fertilizer than grain but more spraying — bollworm, aphids, you have to watch the field all summer. My wife and I pick the cotton by hand, multiple times from September through October. It's hard work but cotton brings better cash than maize if the price holds.

**On money and labor** — I don't have much cash up front, so I buy fertilizer and seed only when I need it. My wife helps full-time, my older son comes back from town to help with wheat and maize harvest, and for cotton picking my daughter-in-law comes too. I don't hire labor except the no-till planter and the harvester — those I pay by the mu.

I don't know if this year will be good or bad. I'll do the same as last year. If a drought comes, I'll irrigate more and spend more on pumping. If prices of fertilizer go up again like they did before, maybe I put down a bit less. But I won't change things much — at my age, experiments lose you money.
